title: We’re ‘the worst’ for spending growth, surging inflation
full_text:
Australia has the worst combination of government spending growth since 2022 and the highest above-target inflation of any G7 country, raising fresh concerns about higher taxes and placing further pressure on the upcoming budget update.
Both Jim Chalmers and Anthony Albanese have been playing down the significance of spending growth and the role it has had in driving inflation, while Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock last week batted away concerns about above-target inflation, saying other countries have lower goals.
However, overall government spending in Australia has increased by about 3.9 per cent of GDP since 2022-23, a faster rate of growth than any of the major advanced economies, according to budget papers and data from the International Monetary Fund.
At the same time, the Reserve Bank’s preferred measure of inflation – core inflation – is 3.7 per cent, the highest in the G7. That inflation rate is also 1.1 per cent above the 2.5 per cent centrepoint of the RBA’s target range, making it the furthest above relevant central bank targets of any of G7 country, according to analysis by the Coalition, verified by The Australian.
Dr Chalmers said last week that Australia was “better placed” than other countries and “we do have a stronger budget than the major advanced economies”. He has also heralded forecasts from the International Monetary Fund predicting Australia’s overall public spending will fall over the next five years.
“By the 2030s it will be lower as a per cent of GDP than all the G7, and revenue lower than five of them until at least the 2030s,” Dr Chalmers said in September before official figures showed federal spending as a percentage of GDP hit 26.9 per cent in financial year 2026, higher than this year’s budget estimated.
The Australian last week revealed the federal budget had been hit by $170bn worth of extra costs over the medium term, in just a five-month period between last year’s MYEFO and the May budget. While details of the $170bn were not revealed, Dr Chalmers dismissed the new number, saying: “It’s entirely normal for the parameters between budget updates to change.” While the Treasurer plays down the government spending levels, which are running at twice the pace of economic growth, Ms Bullock said last week that other countries were grappling with the similar inflationary constraints.
“One point I would make is that if you look at the deviation between target and actual inflation, we don’t look a lot different than some of those countries because our target is 2.5 and theirs is two. So yes, we have a domestic homegrown inflation problem, that is true, and some of those other countries don’t,” Ms Bullock said.
Opposition Treasury spokesman Tim Wilson said there was a clear link between the spending growth and above-target inflation.
“Our Treasurer’s spending addiction is making Australia an international outlier: the biggest spender and the highest inflation of any major advanced economy,” he said.
“That’s not a coincidence. Labor’s spending has pushed up prices, and Australians are paying for it through higher interest rates.
“The Reserve Bank has now said the whispers out loud: domestic pressures were greater than it thought and contributed more to inflation. Government spending is one of the biggest domestic pressures in the economy, and Jim Chalmers can no longer pretend otherwise.
“Every extra dollar of government spending that fuels inflation lands on the kitchen table as a higher mortgage repayment. With rates now at 4.85 per cent, families are paying the price for Labor’s spending addiction.” Antipodean Macro chief economist Justin Fabo said Australia’s position “hinted” at the link between spending and inflation.
“Everyone knows government spending is playing a role in inflation being above target,” Mr Fabo said, “But I also think the issue of government can be a bit overdone.
“This data does hint that government spending plays a role and even though it shows we are an outlier, we are not that much different to other countries.” While growth in spending is high, the level of expenditure as a percentage of GDP is 39.8 per cent, according to the IMF, much lower than the 46.2 per cent average across G7 economies.
Analysis from E61 economists shows that at current spending projections, the government would rely more heavily on bracket creep to raise tax, but that it should not do this.
E61’s Michael Brennan, Richard Holden, Greg Kaplan, Matthew Maltman and Matt Nolan showed that based on this year’s federal budget forecasts of a return to surplus in eight years, half of the improvement would rely on spending cuts, and the other half from higher revenue, “largely due to inflation and wage growth causing taxpayers to pay higher average tax rates”.
The economists said that using bracket creep “cannot resolve Australia’s fiscal sustainability concerns”, because the higher taxes fall unevenly across Australian income earners.
“Workers earning $45,000 per year today would experience sharp increases in tax rates if bracket creep is not addressed over the next decade. The average tax rate of those earning $45,000 will rise by more than five percentage points, from 10.8 per cent to 15.9 per cent by 2035,” the economists estimate. “This is because each pay rise pushes a growing share of their earnings into the 30 per cent tax bracket, which starts at $45,000. The result is that a worker on $45,000 will lose over half (56 per cent) of their disposable pay rises to bracket creep by 2034-35.”
